Stage 3 · Grammar

Verb + -ing, verb + to

Two verbs in a row. The first one decides what the second one looks like.

Read these four sentences from the text you are going to read.
  • She hated going to the office.
  • He chose to study engineering.
  • She has never regretted leaving law.
  • He decided to teach music instead.
What decides whether the second verb is -ing or to?
Which verbs take which
verb + -ingverb + to
The verbsenjoy · hate · like · love · don’t mind · finish · keep · avoid · miss · regret · give up · practise · suggestwant · decide · choose · hope · plan · need · learn · agree · offer · promise · expect · refuse · would like
ExampleShe enjoys teaching more than she expected.He decided to teach music.
NegativeShe avoided telling her family.She didn’t want to spend another decade there.
Both, same meaningstart · begin · continue · prefer — She began studying = She began to study
Both, different meaningstop smoking = you no longer smoke  ·  stop to smoke = you stop in order to smoke
remember locking the door = you have the memory  ·  remember to lock it = do not forget
After a prepositionalways -ing: Instead of looking for another job…  ·  good at playing  ·  interested in teaching
Past Simple recycledonly the first verb changes: He decided to teach, not He decided to taught

THE HONEST RULE. There is no rule. The first verb decides, and the two lists have to be learned. Point at the table, drill the common ones, move on.

ONE THING THAT IS REGULAR. After a preposition it is always -ing: instead of looking, good at playing, tired of waiting.

The mistake to watch: only the first verb carries the tense. He decided to teach, never He decided to taught.

THE HONEST RULE. When two verbs come together, the first verb decides the shape of the second. There is no rule that predicts which verb takes which pattern — the two lists in the table have to be learned, a few at a time.

THE THREE THAT CHANGE MEANING. Stop smoking means you no longer smoke; stop to smoke means you stopped in order to have a cigarette. Remember locking the door means you have the memory; remember to lock it is an instruction. Try opening the window is an experiment; try to open it means it is difficult.

AFTER A PREPOSITION, ALWAYS -ING. Instead of looking, interested in teaching, good at playing, tired of waiting. This one is completely regular, so use it.

Two mistakes to watch: He decided to taught (only the first verb takes the tense) and I enjoy to swim (enjoy is on the -ing list).

You will need these patterns again in Lesson 11, where plan to, hope to and look forward to all describe the future.

Full grammar reference — Verb + -ing and verb + to

Form

+ -ingenjoy · avoid · finish · give up · keep · mind · practise · suggest · can’t stand
+ todecide · want · hope · plan · promise · learn · would like · need · offer · agree
After a prepositionalways -ing: interested in learning · instead of changing · good at cooking
Either, same meaninglike · love · hate · start · begin · continue
NegativeI decided not to go. · She gave up trying.

Spelling and sound

-ing: stop → stopping, take → taking, travel → travelling.

When and why we use it

  • The first verb decides the form of the second one. There is no rule that predicts it — the pairs are learned together.
  • After every preposition (in, at, of, about, after, without) the verb takes -ing.
  • To + verb also answers the question why?: She went to the shop to buy bread.
  • Learn each new verb with its pattern, the way you learn a word with its translation.

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • I enjoy to read. → I enjoy reading.Enjoy + -ing.
  • I decided going. → I decided to go.Decide + to.
  • She is good at to cook. → She is good at cooking.After a preposition, -ing.
  • He gave up to smoke. → He gave up smoking.Give up + -ing.

Don’t confuse it with

Stop smoking = you no longer smoke. Stop to smoke = you pause in order to smoke. At this level, use the first.

Stage 5 · Main input

Reading

Three people who started again, and none of them planned to.

Before you read: at what age is it too late to change career completely?

Choose one. Then read and see whether the text agrees with you.

No right answer yet. This is your opinion.

Three people who started again

Most people decide on a career in their twenties and stop thinking about it. These three did the opposite.

Nadia was a lawyer for eleven years. She was good at it, but she hated going to the office. At thirty-four she left home for the first time in her life, moved to another city and started training to become a nurse. “I didn’t want to spend another decade doing something I disliked,” she says. She finished her training in her late thirties and now works nights in a children’s hospital. She has never regretted leaving law.

Tomas took up the guitar when he was a teenager. He kept playing all through university, but he chose to study engineering because it seemed safer. He worked as an engineer until he was forty-two. Then his company closed. Instead of looking for another job, he decided to teach music. He now performs in a small concert hall twice a month and enjoys teaching more than he expected.

Grace is the oldest of the three. She retired at sixty-one and immediately got bored. She avoided telling her family, but she missed working. So, in her sixties, she began studying again — and last year she qualified as a conductor. She hopes to lead a full orchestra before she is seventy.

None of them planned to change direction. All three would do it again.

Their advice is similar. Expect to feel foolish for about a year. Avoid asking people who have never changed anything. And do not give up doing something you love just because somebody tells you it is not a real job.
